_about: Editorial classification of the UK experiments: category, design type, a one-line
description, and what each was verified against. This file holds ONLY what cannot be
derived from the recipes or the data.
The 28 TESS experiments are NOT here. Their category already ships in
data/catalog/tess_uk_foundation_sources.csv, joined on study_id, and duplicating it
would create exactly the drift that uk_dataverse_provenance.json just suffered — two
places holding the same fact, one of them going stale unnoticed. Row counts,
participant counts, licences and source are likewise derived, never typed.
scripts/experiments_table.py turns this plus those derived facts into
docs/EXPERIMENTS.md. tests/test_experiment_manifest.py fails if a built recipe has
neither a TESS category nor an entry here, so an experiment cannot be added without

_note: The first six are TESS's own categories, reused word-for-word so coverage can be compared
across the two layers rather than across two taxonomies. The two political categories
are additions: the UK layer is overwhelmingly political and TESS's vocabulary has no
political category at all, which is itself a finding about how different the two
corpora are. These are judgements, recorded here so they can be argued with.
The dividing line drawn between the two political categories: IDENTITY/POLARISATION
is about how people regard each OTHER across the Leave/Remain divide, so the outcome
is a judgement of a person. PREFERENCES/POLICY is about what people want GOVERNMENT
to do, so the outcome is a judgement of a policy. 35M5CV's two conjoints both ask a
respondent to pick a PERSON; EFXNLX asks them to pick a DEAL.
_category_vocabulary.cross-national: Same instrument fielded in several countries.
_category_vocabulary.economics/behavioural: Risk, money, time preference, economic judgement.
_category_vocabulary.political identity/polarisation: How people regard each other across a political divide — the outcome is a judgement of a person.
_category_vocabulary.political preferences/policy: What people want government to do — the outcome is a judgement of a policy.
_category_vocabulary.survey methodology: The instrument itself is the object of study.
_category_vocabulary.work/family/gender: Employment, caregiving, gender and family roles.

35M5CV_bbc.description: Forced choice between two applicants for Director General of the BBC, described by name, age, experience, degree, party politics, EU referendum vote and occupation. Tests whether Leave/Remain identity affects judgement of competence for a public role.
35M5CV_bbc.design: paired-profile conjoint, 7 attributes, 5 rounds per respondent
35M5CV_bbc.verified_against: the authors' own `cregg::cj()` run over the raw deposit, transcribed to data/catalog/answer_key_35M5CV_bbc.csv

35M5CV_lodger.description: Forced choice between two prospective lodgers described by name, age, occupation, volunteering, party politics, EU referendum vote and hobby. The classic social-distance measure: would you share your home with someone who voted the other way.
35M5CV_lodger.design: paired-profile conjoint, 7 attributes, 5 rounds per respondent
35M5CV_lodger.verified_against: the authors' own `cregg::cj()` run over the raw deposit, transcribed to data/catalog/answer_key_35M5CV_lodger.csv

35M5CV_sky.description: Five-item battery measuring strength of emotional attachment to one's own Brexit identity (Leaver/Remainer) or party identity (Conservative/Labour) — in-group language, personal offence at criticism, felt commonality, connectedness and pride in one's own side. The in-group-identification component of affective polarization, restricted to respondents with a clean primary identity (excludes 'Neither'/'None' respondents routed into a battery via an undocumented follow-up question).
35M5CV_sky.design: randomised split ballot (Brexit identity vs party identity elicitation), 5 items per respondent, 2,411 respondents x 5 items
35M5CV_sky.verified_against: the paper's own Table 2 — all four identity-group scale means, weighted by the deposit's own `Weights` column, reproduced to the paper's printed 1dp precision; see scripts/verify_35M5CV_sky.py

6MRVOM_brexit_scenario.description: Respondents are told the government will, after Brexit, either keep immigration at roughly current levels or only cut it a little while shifting its source from Europe to beyond Europe. Two outcomes under whichever scenario they met: which party they would support in the next general election, and how satisfied they would feel about the Brexit decision. Tests whether the SOURCE of post-Brexit immigration, not just its level, moves party support and Brexit satisfaction.
6MRVOM_brexit_scenario.design: two-condition between-subject (post-Brexit immigration scenario), 2 outcomes per respondent (11-level nominal party choice, code 12 'Don't know' dropped per the 2026-10-05 ruling; 0-10 satisfaction)
6MRVOM_brexit_scenario.verified_against: no author-computed or published reference exists for this block (checked analysis.R and the full 24-page accepted manuscript); scripts/verify_6MRVOM.py instead confirms the built distribution matches data.sav's own frequency tables exactly, cell for cell

6MRVOM_eu_share.description: Respondents are asked what percentage of all immigrants to the UK they would like to see coming from the EU (vs. elsewhere), on a 0-100 slider; half are additionally told the current EU share is 50%. Tests whether an explicit base-rate anchor shifts the preferred EU/non-EU immigration mix.
6MRVOM_eu_share.design: two-condition between-subject (information anchor present/absent), one outcome on a 0-100 scale
6MRVOM_eu_share.verified_against: the deposit's own analysis.R — svymean(eushare), overall and by condition, reproduced from the built parquet to within rounding

EFXNLX.description: Forced choice between two possible Brexit deals, each described by eight negotiated terms — immigration, EU citizens' rights, trade, legal jurisdiction, budget contributions, payments, the Irish border and the timeline — followed by a 1-4 acceptability rating of each deal separately.
EFXNLX.design: paired-profile conjoint, 8 attributes, 6 rounds per respondent, 3 outcomes per round (1 choice + 2 ratings)
EFXNLX.verified_against: the authors' own `cregg::cj()`, 84 estimates agreeing to 1e-6; data/catalog/answer_key_EFXNLX.csv

LOGVPZ_brexit_satisfaction.description: Respondents are told to imagine they have won a substantial lottery prize, or told nothing, then asked how satisfied they are that the UK voted to leave the EU. Tests whether unearned wealth shifts Brexit support.
LOGVPZ_brexit_satisfaction.design: two-condition between-subject, one outcome on an 11-point scale
LOGVPZ_brexit_satisfaction.verified_against: the paper's own Table D.1 — N, control mean and both regression coefficients

LOGVPZ_risk_tolerance.description: The same lottery-wealth treatment, with the outcome a 0-3 financial risk-tolerance code built from a branching pair of hypothetical job-gamble questions (would you swap a safe job for one with a 50-50 chance of doubling or cutting your income).
LOGVPZ_risk_tolerance.design: two-condition between-subject, one DERIVED outcome on a 0-3 scale
LOGVPZ_risk_tolerance.verified_against: the paper's own Table D.2 — N, control mean and both regression coefficients; the branch logic itself is pinned by tests/test_derive_LOGVPZ.py across all 64 inputs of the instrument's code space

PMV0TG.description: Forced choice between two hypothetical people over who should receive a COVID-19 vaccine first, differing on risk of death, risk of transmitting, income, occupation and age. A rationing problem: who deserves a scarce life-saving good.
PMV0TG.design: paired-profile conjoint, 5 attributes, 8 rounds per respondent
PMV0TG.verified_against: the UK column of the authors' own deposited conjoint_combined_results_UNWEIGHTED_ols.tex — 17 coefficients to within 0.006

POMIFD.description: Respondents see two of 336 political arguments (14 rhetorical elements x 12 policy issues x 2 positions, for/against) shown together, verbatim as extracted from Hansard debate transcripts, and say which they find more persuasive or that the two are about the same. The respondent judges which ARGUMENT about a policy is persuasive, not a person — closer to the 'policy' pole than the 'identity' pole, since nothing about Leave/Remain regard for other people is measured. Unlike every other UK Dataverse study in this corpus (all conjoints, where the condition is a table of attribute levels this project renders into prose), the condition text here is the fielded instrument's own argument text, transcribed verbatim and not authored by this project.
POMIFD.design: within-subject paired-argument forced choice, 3-way nominal outcome (argument one more persuasive / about the same / argument two more persuasive), 4 comparisons per respondent drawn from 12 policy issues
POMIFD.verified_against: the paper's own published descriptive statistic (AJPS 2022, p.9) — '28% of comparisons... about the same' — reproduced from the built parquet's response distribution; scripts/verify_POMIFD.py. Does NOT verify the headline Bayesian multilevel model (not refit) or any individual argument's text/pairing, which an aggregate proportion cannot see — see the script's own docstring

PZB01G.description: Respondents are shown a campaign vignette combining a pro- or anti-EU cultural frame, a pro- or anti-EU economic frame and a pro- or anti-EU political frame (eight combinations), or no vignette at all (a true control), then asked how they would vote in the EU membership referendum. Tests which real-world campaign arguments, alone and in combination, shift referendum vote intention.
PZB01G.design: 2x2x2 full factorial (cultural x economic x political frame, each pro/anti) plus a true control, one outcome on a 4-way nominal scale (Remain/Leave/Would not vote/Don't know)
PZB01G.verified_against: the paper's own Appendix Table A6 (nine group sizes, reproduced exactly) and its own text (p.8, the control group's published Wave 2 Remain/Leave/Don't-know-or-would-not-vote shares, reproduced to 0.1 percentage point); scripts/verify_PZB01G.py

QQM5MC.description: A split ballot crossing a Leaver/Remainer identity prime with factual information about UK GDP growth. Outcomes are the respondent's estimate of the UK's growth rank among 34 OECD countries, and whether they think the economy is getting better or worse. Tests motivated reasoning about shared economic facts.
QQM5MC.design: 2x2 split ballot (prime x information) plus a true control, 2 outcomes
QQM5MC.verified_against: the paper's own Table 1 and Figures 4-5 — eight group means and two Ns

RJTVG8.description: Forced choice between two hypothetical UK internet-voting (i-voting) policies, differing on ten features — pre-registration, voting method, voting window, where trials succeeded, the pilot's effect on turnout and on fraud risk, who controls the platform, the cost to government, the proposing party and the endorsing body. The respondent judges a PROPOSED POLICY, not a person.
RJTVG8.design: paired-profile conjoint, 10 attributes (one — platform — a single 6-level draw, not a 2x3 cross), 5 tasks per respondent
RJTVG8.verified_against: the authors' own cregg::mm() marginal means, Table A.4 of the author-accepted manuscript — 51 estimates to within 0.0015

ukds_6849_vig_housework_w5.description: Respondents imagine themselves in a couple and rate how satisfied they would be with how the housework is shared. Five dimensions are randomised: whose job is full or part time, whose hourly pay is higher, whether there is a child and its age, how the housework splits between them, and whether paid help is employed. The respondent is INSIDE the scenario -- the wording is "Imagine that you are married or cohabiting" -- so the outcome is imagined own satisfaction, not judgement of a described couple. Wave 5 (2012).
ukds_6849_vig_housework_w5.design: 4x3x4x5x2 full factorial = 480 cells, all 480 occurring (6-39 rows each). Three scenarios per respondent, drawn without replacement, allocated per HOUSEHOLD: both partners in a couple rate the identical three arrangements. One outcome, 7-point satisfaction.
ukds_6849_vig_housework_w5.verified_against: NOT verified against a publication -- the Innovation Panel User Guide cites none for this experiment, so there is no published answer key and none is claimed. What IS verified: (a) the User Guide's own documented design, including its claim that "the exact allocation at Wave 5 was replicated at Wave 6" -- 27,696 of 27,705 allocation cells identical for the 1,849 people in both waves; (b) the household join, against wave 5's duplicate person-level copy of four of the five dimensions, 23,880 comparisons, zero disagreements (scripts/gen_ip_vig_housework.py --check); (c) all 480 cells present and no respondent drawing one twice; (d) the five marginals flat to within 3 points of uniform in both waves; (e) the row counts, 4,550 and 5,081, reached independently by a standalone builder and by the recipe pipeline. tests/test_ip_vig_housework.py

ukds_6849_vig_ageing_w9.description: Respondents read three descriptions of an imaginary 75-year-old and rate how successfully each is ageing, 0-10. Six life dimensions are randomised per description -- long-term illness (none or diabetes), difficulty climbing stairs, problems remembering, opening food packaging, how often they see family and friends, and volunteering -- and the name (George, Harry, Margaret or Anne), which sets the pronouns and is named in the question. The respondent judges ANOTHER person, so the outcome is social perception of ageing, not self-report. Wave 9 (2016).
ukds_6849_vig_ageing_w9.design: 4 names x 2^6 = 256 cells, all 256 occurring. Three descriptions per respondent, each with its own allocation; within-subject, so each outcome names its own condition_vars. Self-completion only (web, or face-to-face respondents who took the self-completion section). One outcome, 0-10. Allocation clean: 2,010 distinct allocations among 2,010 respondents. Undocumented constraint: descriptions 1 and 2 never share all six life codes.
ukds_6849_vig_ageing_w9.verified_against: NOT verified against a publication -- the Innovation Panel User Guide cites none for 9.18, so no answer key is claimed. What IS verified: (a) every derived per-slot name against the archive's own labels (scripts/gen_ip_vig_ageing.py --check: 6,030 names in wave 9 against each slot's labels, 6,660 in wave 17 against the name-sequence labels, zero disagreements), and wave 9's per-slot names produce exactly the guide's six name sequences; (b) on every built row, the pronouns and the question agree with the name the description opens with, against a table written from the questionnaire rather than the recipe; (c) every factor a row claims is expressed in its condition text; (d) all 256 cells present; (e) row counts, 5,967 and 6,600, reached by the generator's count and by the pipeline; (g) an independent checker re-transcribed both questionnaires and re-rendered every one of the 12,567 rows from the raw files: 0 condition, 0 outcome, 0 name and 0 dimension-code disagreements. tests/test_ip_vig_ageing.py

The respondent judges ANOTHER person, so the outcome is social perception of ageing, not self-report. Wave 17 (2024). Wording identical to wave 9 but for one comma.
ukds_6849_vig_ageing_w17.design: 4 names x 2^6 = 256 cells, all 256 occurring. Three descriptions per respondent, each with its own allocation; within-subject, so each outcome names its own condition_vars. Self-completion only (web, or face-to-face respondents who took the self-completion section). One outcome, 0-10. ALLOCATION NOT AS DOCUMENTED: 354 of 2,220 respondents (all web, late fieldwork) share one identical allocation, and 933 in all share theirs with someone (1,497 distinct). 681 rows (10%) carry no age or sex. Each row's condition is what that person read, but the design is not a balanced factorial; see the recipe notes.
ukds_6849_vig_ageing_w17.verified_against: NOT verified against a publication -- the Innovation Panel User Guide cites none for 9.18, so no answer key is claimed. What IS verified: (a) every derived per-slot name against the archive's own labels (scripts/gen_ip_vig_ageing.py --check: 6,030 names in wave 9 against each slot's labels, 6,660 in wave 17 against the name-sequence labels, zero disagreements), and wave 9's per-slot names produce exactly the guide's six name sequences; (b) on every built row, the pronouns and the question agree with the name the description opens with, against a table written from the questionnaire rather than the recipe; (c) every factor a row claims is expressed in its condition text; (d) all 256 cells present; (e) row counts, 5,967 and 6,600, reached by the generator's count and by the pipeline; (g) an independent checker re-transcribed both questionnaires and re-rendered every one of the 12,567 rows from the raw files: 0 condition, 0 outcome, 0 name and 0 dimension-code disagreements. (f) the allocation anomaly, recomputed by the generator and pinned in tests. tests/test_ip_vig_ageing.py

ukds_6849_vig_flexstigma_w16.description: Respondents in work, aged 18-65, imagine they are an HR manager filling a full-time team-lead post and rate three internal candidates, each on four 0-10 questions: would they recommend the candidate, and how do they see the candidate's work commitment, productivity and team-playing. Each candidate varies on gender (through the name and pronouns), parenthood, their own home working, how common home working is in the company, and the company's hybrid-working policy. The question the design asks is whether home working is stigmatised, and more so for mothers. Wave 16 (2023).
ukds_6849_vig_flexstigma_w16.design: 6 names (two per slot) x 2 x 3 x 4 x 4 = 576 cells, 192 per slot, all occurring. Three candidates per respondent, four outcomes each (twelve tasks), within-subject. Allocation clean: 1,616 distinct allocations among 1,616 respondents.
ukds_6849_vig_flexstigma_w16.verified_against: NOT yet verified against the published chapter (Chung & Wang 2024, ISER working paper 2024-11, pp. 105-123): its PDF sits behind a browser check this machine could not pass. What IS verified: (a) every derived name against its slot's own archive labels (scripts/gen_ip_vig_flexstigma.py --check: 4,848 names, zero disagreements); (b) on every row, the description opens with the candidate's name and the pronouns and all twelve questions agree with it, against a table written from the questionnaire rather than the recipe; (c) every factor a row claims is expressed in its condition; (d) all 576 cells present, each slot showing only its own names; (e) 17,656 rows, reached by the generator's count and by the pipeline. (f) an independent checker transcribed the questionnaire itself and re-rendered every row from the raw file: 17,656 = 17,656, 0 condition, 0 outcome, 0 response, 0 name and 0 pronoun disagreements. tests/test_ip_vig_flexstigma.py

ukds_6849_alcohol_w15.description: Respondents who had drunk alcohol in the past year report how much they drink on a typical drinking day and how often they binge, with the questions worded in UNITS of alcohol (the NHS version) or in ALCOHOLIC DRINKS. The binge threshold is 6 or more for women and 8 or more for men. The rows teach whether the same person reports differently when asked in units, which few people count in. Wave 15 (2022).
ukds_6849_alcohol_w15.design: Two-version question-wording split, allocated by household (1,367 / 1,352). Two outcomes per respondent, each asked in their own version's wording; the condition is narrated as 'You were asked: "..."' (the rpw4u precedent). 5-point banded answers.
ukds_6849_alcohol_w15.verified_against: NOT verified against a publication -- the User Guide cites none for 9.36. What IS verified: (a) the household join, by the data's own structure: all 4,208 answers sit in the respondent's own version's variables and none in the other's (scripts/gen_ip_alcohol.py --check), and a scrambled join fails it; (b) on every row, the question is its version's own, word-for-word against a table written from the questionnaire, and the 6-or-8 threshold matches the respondent's sex (0 mismatches in 2,112 binge rows); (c) 4,208 rows, reached by the generator's count and the pipeline. tests/test_ip_alcohol.py

ukds_6849_eq5d5l_w11.description: Respondents describe their own health today on the five EQ-5D items (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) in the 5-level form, the NICE-recommended quality-of-life measure. The condition is whether they had already answered the 3L form earlier in the same interview. Wave 11 (2018).
ukds_6849_eq5d5l_w11.design: Order experiment (eq5dcond, three arms) built on prior exposure: two conditions, 3L asked earlier or not. Arms differing only by module position share a condition. 70 respondents allocated to see the 3L first who skipped the early module are excluded. Five outcomes per respondent, each listing its 5 options word-for-word.
ukds_6849_eq5d5l_w11.verified_against: NOT verified against a publication -- the User Guide cites none for 9.24. What IS verified: (a) every row's condition against what the raw file says the respondent was actually routed into, not what was allocated; (b) every response against the raw value in the module its arm used; (c) each question's options against a table written from the questionnaire; (d) 13,203 rows, reached by the generator's count and the pipeline. tests/test_ip_eq5d.py

ukds_6849_eq5d3l_w11.description: Respondents describe their own health today on the five EQ-5D items (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) in the 3-level form, the NICE-recommended quality-of-life measure. The condition is whether they had already answered the 5L form earlier in the same interview. Wave 11 (2018).

ukds_6849_identity_w2.description: Respondents say how important their occupation, or in the other version their profession, is to their sense of who they are: important, not very important, or not at all important. One word varies between households, from an identity battery adapted from the 2007-08 Citizenship Survey. Interviewer-administered. Wave 2 (2009).
ukds_6849_identity_w2.design: Two-version one-word split ballot, allocated by household. One outcome per respondent (item (a) of a 13-item battery; the other twelve are identical across versions and not built). Condition narrated as 'You were asked: ...'.
ukds_6849_identity_w2.verified_against: NOT verified against a publication -- the User Guide cites none for 9.4. What IS verified: (a) the household join against indresp's own copy of the allocation, 1,788 comparisons, zero disagreements, and no answer in the other version's variable (scripts/gen_ip_identity.py --check; a scrambled join fails it); (b) every row's condition and question against the stem and item written from the questionnaire; (c) 1,746 rows, reached by the generator's count and the pipeline. tests/test_ip_identity.py

ukds_6849_itemcount_w8.description: Respondents see six lists of statements about who they have been attracted to, who they have had a sexual experience with, and how they would describe themselves, and report only HOW MANY are true for them. Three of the lists carry one extra, sensitive statement ('is the same sex as me'; 'gay, lesbian or bisexual'), a technique for measuring what people will not say directly. Wave 8 (2015).
ukds_6849_itemcount_w8.design: Item-count (list) experiment: which three lists carry the sensitive statement depends on the household's group and flips between waves 8 and 9. Six outcomes per respondent, each a count; statements rendered in the respondent's own shuffled order (ItemOverride.line_order_vars).
ukds_6849_itemcount_w8.verified_against: NOT verified against a publication -- the User Guide cites none for 9.17. What IS verified: (a) every answer sits in a list the respondent's group was shown and none elsewhere (scripts/gen_ip_itemcount.py --check); (b) every row's list, stem and sensitive statement against wording written from the questionnaire, which wave 8 and wave 9 share word-for-word; (c) every row's statement order against the raw permutation code; (d) 12,672 rows, reached by the generator's count and the pipeline. tests/test_ip_itemcount.py

ukds_6849_reqol_w14.description: Respondents describe their mental and physical wellbeing on the ReQoL-10 (ten items plus physical health) and EQ-5D-3L, standard quality-of-life and psychological-distress measures. The condition is whether they had already answered the GHQ-12 earlier in the same interview. Wording follows the respondent's mode (web, face-to-face self-completion or telephone). Wave 14 (2021).
ukds_6849_reqol_w14.design: Order experiment (two arms) built on prior exposure: two conditions, the other block asked earlier or not. The arm comes from n_req10cond for continuing households and n_ff_req10cond for the refreshment sample, whose person-level value is meaningless (ledger 134). Each question lists its options word-for-word.
ukds_6849_reqol_w14.verified_against: NOT verified against a publication -- the User Guide cites none for 9.31. What IS verified: (a) every row's condition against which early module the respondent actually answered, independent of either allocation variable, and a build trusting the person-level variable fails it; (b) every response against the raw value in the module its arm used; (c) the ReQoL and EQ-5D wording against the respondent's mode; (d) 48,548 rows, reached by the generator's count and the pipeline. (e) an independent checker re-rendered every row from raw with its own transcription; it found the telephone EQ-5D options wrongly in the self-completion wording, since fixed and pinned by a test. tests/test_ip_reqol.py
